questionText:
Each of a set of $n$ processes executes the following code using two semaphores a and b initialized to 1 and 0, respectively. Assume that count is a shared variable initialized to 0 and not used in CODE SECTION P.

CODE SECTION P

wait(a); count=count+1;
if (count==n) signal(b);
signal(a); wait(b); signal(b);

CODE SECTION Q

What does the code achieve?
options: It ensures that no process executes CODE SECTION Q before every process has finished CODE SECTION P.
It ensures that at most two processes are in CODE SECTION Q at any time.
It ensures that all processes execute CODE SECTION P mutually exclusively.
It ensures that at most $n-1$ processes are in CODE SECTION P at any time.
explanation:
Step 1: Analyze initialization and variables
Semaphore $a$ is initialized to $1$ (acts as a mutex for updating $count$).
Semaphore $b$ is initialized to $0$ (acts as a barrier turnstile).
Variable $count$ is initialized to $0$ to track how many processes have completed CODE SECTION P.

Step 2: Trace process execution
1. The first $n-1$ processes execute CODE SECTION P, acquire lock $a$, increment $count$, release $a$, and then call wait(b). Since $b = 0$, all $n-1$ processes block at wait(b).
2. When the $n^{\text{th}}$ process finishes CODE SECTION P, it acquires lock $a$, increments $count$ to $n$, and triggers if (count == n) signal(b);.
3. This $n^{\text{th}}$ process executes signal(b), incrementing $b$ to $1$, then releases $a$.

Step 3: Barrier release mechanism
4. The $n^{\text{th}}$ process passes wait(b) and immediately calls signal(b), which unblocks another waiting process.
5. This creates a cascading chain reaction (turnstile pattern), allowing all $n$ processes to sequentially pass wait(b) and proceed to CODE SECTION Q.

Conclusion:
No process can execute CODE SECTION Q until all $n$ processes have completed CODE SECTION P and incremented $count$ to $n$. Thus, Option (A) is correct.
